definition: The Baltic sky god, the bright heaven and the highest power in the pantheon. Lithuanian dievas and Latvian dievs also mean 'God' in Christian usage, so the older figure and the Christian one are difficult to separate.

The trickster and devil of Baltic folklore, known as velnias in Lithuanian and velns in Latvian. In creation tales he dives for earth and spoils the flat world; in Christian times he becomes the devil, but older traits survive.

The Baltic thunder god, called Pērkons in Latvian. He rides the storm, carries an axe and strikes the oak, and his spring thunder brings rain. Chronicles, dainas and place names make him the best-attested Baltic deity.

A Baltic folk song, especially the Latvian four-line daina. Dainas cover courtship, weddings, work, orphans, the sun and the dead; tens of thousands were recorded, and they are the main evidence for Baltic myth.

The sea goddess of the Lithuanian amber legend, ruler of a palace beneath the Baltic. She loves the fisherman Kastytis; Perkūnas shatters the palace, and amber is read as the fragments or her tears. The popular story is largely literary.

The heroine of a Lithuanian folktale, 'Eglė the Queen of Serpents'. She marries the serpent Žilvinas, is betrayed by her brothers, and is transformed into a spruce while her children become trees. Her name means spruce.

The legendary first teacher of Baltic funeral rites, known from a Slavonic chronograph of 1261. He passes the gates of the dead, tests burial in earth, tree and fire, and establishes cremation. His myth is the oldest recorded Baltic narrative.

Fossil resin from the Baltic coast, called gintaras in Lithuanian and dzintars in Latvian. It has been traded since prehistory and is central to the Jūratė legend, where the stones are the ruins of her palace or her tears.

The Lithuanian name for the heavenly land of the blessed dead, sometimes imagined beyond a mountain, a river or a gate. Dausos is a place of light and rest, and the word also carries the sense of 'paradise'.

The Grand Duchy of Lithuania before its conversion in 1387, and Samogitia before 1413. It was the last pagan state in Europe, fought by the Teutonic Order and later romanticised as a time of sacred oaks, fire and song.
